summary: Provides a framework of scenarios and requirements for pseudowire (PW) redundancy. A set of redundant pseudowires is configured between provider edge nodes, and the nodes need to agree on which one carries traffic. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A pseudowire carries an emulated service across a packet network. This document explains how a service can keep a backup pseudowire ready and how the network can choose which path forwards traffic.

questions: how does a standby pseudowire work
subtitle: A framework for selecting backup pseudowires when a service path fails.

tldr.problem: A failed attachment circuit, provider edge, or segment-switching node can interrupt a service carried over a pseudowire.
tldr.mechanism: The framework describes redundant pseudowires and an active-or-standby Preferential Forwarding Status so provider edge nodes can select a forwarding path.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides reference scenarios and generic requirements for protection switching and operations. It does not specify the signaling mechanism itself.

today: RFC 6718 is an Informational framework published in August 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC leaves the signaling mechanisms to other specifications.

sections.title: Why Pseudowire Redundancy Is Needed
sections.content:
Pseudowire redundancy aims to preserve an emulated service when a component in its path fails or a backup component is activated. It uses redundant attachment circuits, provider edge nodes, and pseudowires. The framework keeps only one path between customer edge nodes active at a time; permanent duplication of traffic is outside its scope.

Protection in the packet-switched network can cover some tunnel failures, but it cannot cover every provider edge or remote attachment-circuit failure. Redundant pseudowires supplement that protection. The document also says a failure on one side should not be propagated to attachment circuits on the other side or to customer edge nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: A backup pseudowire can keep a service connected when a link or provider edge fails. The framework uses one forwarding path at a time and coordinates the change between its endpoints.

sections.title: Active, Standby, and Forwarding Status
sections.content:
An active pseudowire carries user, control-plane, and operations traffic. A standby pseudowire is configured and available but does not carry user traffic; it may carry operations and some control traffic. The primary pseudowire is the locally preferred one when revertive behavior is configured.

The RFC introduces a Preferential Forwarding Status of active or standby. This is separate from whether the pseudowire is operationally up or down. Communicating this forwarding status lets the provider edge nodes agree on which member of a redundant set should carry traffic; the signaling details are outside the document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: An active pseudowire carries user traffic, while a standby one is ready but waits. The forwarding-status flag tells the endpoints which one to use.

sections.title: Reference Network Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC presents six example topologies that can be combined. They cover one or two dual-homed customer edge nodes, redundant multi-segment pseudowires protecting segment-switching nodes, hierarchical VPLS protection, a VPLS ring, and network-facing provider edge protection.

Across the scenarios, the endpoints use active and standby status to make the forwarding path consistent. In a ring, status exchange can let both ends block a pseudowire group. In the network-facing provider edge example, status can also avoid unnecessary replication of multicast, broadcast, and unknown-unicast frames across core pseudowires.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples apply the same active-or-standby idea to several network layouts. In each case, the provider edge nodes need a consistent choice of the path carrying traffic.

sections.title: Protection and Operational Requirements
sections.content:
One-to-one protection must be supported; N-to-one protection should be supported. Non-revertive switching must be supported, while returning to a preferred primary pseudowire after recovery is optional. Switching must be possible through manual or forced action and through a signal failure, with failure triggers given lower priority than manual or forced triggers.

Provider edge nodes should detect inconsistent settings for primary and secondary pseudowires or switching mode. If they cannot resolve an inconsistency automatically, they must raise an alarm. They must support configuration of the switching mode when both modes are implemented, and management information must support monitoring the redundancy configuration across packet networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements make a one-to-one backup and non-revertive switching mandatory. Operators also need a way to configure protection and be alerted when the endpoints disagree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The redundancy method requires an extension to the pseudowire setup and maintenance protocol, which is carried over the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). The RFC says the method inherits the security mechanisms of the LDP version implemented by the provider edge nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Redundancy signaling uses the pseudowire setup system carried over LDP. Its security depends on the LDP mechanisms implemented by the provider edge nodes.
